title: The Human Stain
full_review:
����������� Tragic histories and long-held secrets unravel when an aging professor gets entangled in an affair with an angry young woman in "The Human Stain" (Miramax).

Philip Roth's novel gets silver-screen treatment under director Robert Benton's able hands, although Nicholas Meyer's screenplay is sometimes curiously flat. Nonetheless, stellar performances by Nicole Kidman and Ed Harris won't allow viewer interest to flag. And, despite its erotic content, at its core it is a tale of compassion gradually transcending lust.

After being wrongly accused in 1998 of a racist remark, longtime New England classics professor Coleman Silk (Anthony Hopkins) angrily resigns. Worse, his wife (Phyllis Newman) becomes so upset she succumbs to a heart attack.

Coleman seeks out local recluse and blocked writer Nathan (Gary Sinese) to write his story. Although the author refuses, Coleman draws him out and the two lonely men forge a friendship. But it is Coleman's chance meeting with hostile blue-collar worker Faunia (Kidman) and their explosive affair that rocks his sedate, elderly existence.

At this point, not very far into the movie, the director chooses to reveal Coleman's shocking (to those not familiar with the novel) secret through a simple flashback to Coleman (Wentworth Miller) in 1948: He is actually a light-skinned African-American. After his white NYU classmate and lover (Jacinda Barrett) rejects him when she learns the truth, he consciously decides to pass as a white Jew, eliminating racial problems in his personal and professional life. Leaving family behind, he tells no one.

Faunia, too, is keeping a painful past locked deep inside. Seeking oblivion in mindless sexual encounters, she refuses to allow Coleman any emotional intimacy whatsoever. However, there is no ignoring the lurking presence of her Vietnam War-scarred ex-husband (Harris) who continues to stalk her, lurching between hating her and needing her.

Little by little, Coleman discovers why Faunia has built such an impregnable wall around herself.

As the stigma of scandal swirls around him -- a retired professor sleeping with a member of the college's janitorial staff who could practically be his granddaughter -- Coleman resolves to share her pain, and perhaps face the betrayals of his own past.

The revelations come, however, in such low-key fashion that they distance the viewer from emotional involvement and at the cost of a certain amount of anticipated suspense.

While Brit Hopkins is a bit difficult to accept as a black man posing as an American Jew, his story fascinates and he wins over our sympathies despite his failings since he is now willing to risk everything for his last love. Aussie Kidman is riveting as chain-smoking, self-described trailer trash lashing out at anyone hoping to crack her brittle facade. Harris is also compelling as the unhinged, grieving veteran determined to end his wife's affair. Sinese brings gravitas to the role as the narrator and observer of events, but is upstaged by the personal crises of the other characters.

There's no doubt that Coleman enters the affair out of Viagra-fueled lust but the movie manages to move beyond its carnal elements and focus on the frail and flawed humanities of its characters. In fact, although the bedroom visuals could have been more discreet, it's soon apparent that Coleman's affairs become just the backdrop to the story of why he felt obliged to sever ties with his family in order not to be always seen as "the Negro professor." Playing his mother is Anna Deavere Smith, whose expression is priceless when young Coleman informs her of his engagement to a white woman, and that he told her his mother is dead.

Elegantly filmed, the perilous relationships are the heart of the story with plenty to chew on afterward about the consequences of avoiding racism at such a terrible cost.

Due to sexual affairs, brief full female nudity, much rough language, boxing ring violence, a racial epithet and minimal profanity and crass expressions, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
